title: The World's Most Decorated Indian Chef Is Finally Opening a Restaurant in India
excerpt: Gaggan Anand, who topped Asia's 50 Best five times running from Bangkok, is bringing Raga to a 42-seat space on Delhi's Janpath — and it might be the most significant Indian restaurant opening in a generation.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Gaggan Anand, a celebrated chef, is opening Raga in New Delhi this summer.
  • Raga will feature 42 seats and focus on Indian ingredients and culinary traditions.
  • India's fine dining scene has matured, making it a prime market for ambitious restaurants.
  • Raga is included in the 2026 World's 50 Best anticipated openings list.
  • Gaggan aims to keep prices around ₹8,000 per person, accessible for fine dining.
Raga: A Culinary Homecoming
›First restaurant in India after two decades.
›Located on Janpath, near India Gate.
›42-seat capacity for an intimate dining experience.
›Focus on Indian ingredients and culinary traditions.
For nearly two decades, the most celebrated Indian chef on the planet has been cooking Indian food everywhere except India. Gaggan Anand — five-time winner of Asia's #1 restaurant, a fixture on the World's 50 Best list, trained under Ferran Adrià at the legendary El Bulli — has built his empire in Bangkok. His eponymous restaurant, *Gaggan*, is a 25-course emoji-menu experience that has redefined how the world thinks about Indian cuisine: molecular, theatrical, irreverent, and technically dazzling. Now, for the first time, he's coming home. ## Raga: A Homecoming in 42 Seats ![India Gate — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/75/India_Gate_%28All_India_War_Memorial%29.jpg) Raga, opening this summer in New Delhi, will be Gaggan Anand's first restaurant in India. Located on Janpath — prime real estate flanked by government buildings, luxury hotels, and historic markets near India Gate — it will seat just 42 people. The name carries a double meaning. In Hindi, *raga* means *sur* — a melodic framework in Indian classical music, a structure that allows infinite improvisation within defined boundaries. It also encodes a partnership: "RA" for Rydo Anton, Gaggan's longtime head chef and collaborator, and "GA" for Gaggan Anand himself. > **"It also encodes a partnership: "RA" for Rydo Anton, Gaggan's longtime head chef and collaborator, and "GA" for Gaggan Anand himself."** "It will stand independently, with its own originality," Gaggan told The Nod magazine. "It will have playfulness, but, above all, it will have complete creative freedom." ## Why Now, After All These Years? Gaggan has been asked this question for years. In a candid interview with Esquire India, he offered a characteristically elliptical answer: "I'm a Pisces. Pisces are mysterious. Like a fish. You can't catch a fish unless you bait it." But the practical reasoning is clearer. India's fine dining scene has matured dramatically. Restaurants like Masque in Mumbai (ranked 15th on Asia's 50 Best) and NAAR in Kasauli have proven that India can sustain ambitious, globally competitive dining. Indians are spending on experiences. The infrastructure — from produce quality to wine culture — has caught up. ![El Bulli — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d6/ElBulli_Ferran_Adri%C3%A0.jpg) "India is the only big market of domestic consumption in fine dining," Gaggan said in a recent interview. "Every restaurant is doing well. I think India is the new China." He also plans to keep prices accessible by Indian fine dining standards, targeting around ₹8,000 per person — a fraction of what a meal at the Bangkok *Gaggan* costs. ## What to Expect on the Plate
India's Fine Dining Evolution
›Restaurants like Masque and NAAR show India's dining potential.
›Gaggan believes India is the new China for fine dining.
›Growing consumer spending on dining experiences.
›Improved infrastructure for produce and wine culture.
Details are still emerging, but Gaggan has hinted at a two-tasting-menu format. Expect his greatest hits: the legendary yoghurt explosion (a riff on El Bulli's olive spherification, reimagined with Indian flavors), the emoji menu format, and the "Lick it Up" curries that made him famous. Being in India, however, will give him something he has never had before: direct access to local produce, seasonal ingredients, and the culinary traditions he grew up with. ![New Delhi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg/3840px-Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg) "I felt it is high time. I would love to cook Indian food with Indian ingredients," he said. "I did a few pop-ups across the country to understand India and connect to the roots of my country and culture." ## The Diaspora Watches For NRIs who have followed Gaggan's rise — watching his Netflix *Chef's Table* episode, tracking his rankings, planning Bangkok trips around his reservation windows — Raga carries an emotional charge that transcends food criticism. Here is a Kolkata-born chef who left India, conquered the world's most competitive culinary stage, and is now returning to cook for the country that shaped his palate. In an era when Indian talent is increasingly recognized globally but often has to leave home to be recognized, Gaggan's homecoming is symbolic.
Raga's Anticipated Impact
›Included in 2026 World's 50 Best anticipated openings.
›Symbolic return of a globally recognized Indian chef.
›Emotional significance for NRIs and Indian culinary culture.
›Reservations expected to be highly sought after.
World's 50 Best Restaurants included Raga on its 2026 list of the most anticipated new openings worldwide, alongside restaurants from some of the planet's most decorated chefs. The 42 seats at Raga will be among the hardest reservations to get in Asia. But for the Indian food world, the significance is bigger than any waitlist: one of its greatest exports is finally coming home.
